observation: Chernev, Böckenholt & Goodman (2015, J. Consumer Psychology) meta-analysed 99 effect-size observations (N=7,202) on choice overload and found the average effect on satisfaction/regret was small but reliably moderated by four factors: choice-set complexity (harder-to-compare alternatives increase overload), decision-task difficulty (e.g. time pressure increases overload), preference uncertainty (not knowing how to weigh attributes increases overload), and decision goal (weak commitment to choosing increases overload).
claim: More options are not intrinsically harmful; overload appears specifically when alternatives are hard to compare, the chooser is uncertain of their own preferences, or they are not seriously committed to deciding — conditions a comparison UI can directly reduce (alignable attributes, low task difficulty) rather than needing to hide options.
mechanism: Overload arises from the cost side of the evaluation (comparison difficulty, ambiguity about how to weigh attributes) rather than sheer count; reducing comparison cost per alternative should reduce overload even at constant set size.
population: general adult consumers, meta-analysis of lab and field studies
context: meta-analysis, mostly consumer choice lab/field experiments

implications.text: A decision-table feature should make alternatives alignable (same attributes as rows/columns) and reduce comparison difficulty, rather than simply truncating the option list — this addresses the actual moderators of overload.

observation: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (2010, J. Consumer Research) meta-analysed 50 experiments (63 conditions, N=5,036) on choice overload and found a mean effect size of essentially zero with large between-study heterogeneity; a substantial share of studies found no overload or found more options helped.
claim: The 'more choices hurt' effect (including the famous jam-display study) does not reliably replicate at the population level; choice overload is conditional/moderator-dependent, not a general law.
mechanism: unknown / heterogeneous — consistent with Chernev's later claim that overload only appears under specific moderating conditions rather than universally.
context: meta-analysis of lab and field choice experiments

implications.text: Do not default to aggressively hiding/limiting options 'because choice overload'; only invest overload-mitigation UI effort when the moderating conditions (complex/unalignable attributes, time pressure, preference uncertainty, weak commitment) are actually present.

observation: The Cochrane systematic review of patient decision aids (Stacey et al., most recent full update 2017/2024, 105 trials, N=31,043) found high-quality evidence that decision aids reduce 'feeling uninformed' and decisional conflict related to feeling uninformed/unclear values, and in 8 of 10 studies measuring it, increased values-choice congruence, with no evidence of adverse effects on outcomes or satisfaction versus usual care.
claim: Structured decision aids (options laid out with pros/cons/probabilities tied to the decider's own values) reliably improve a person's sense of being informed and increase the chance the chosen option matches their stated values/preferences, at no measured cost.
mechanism: Decision aids externalise the comparison structure and probabilistic outcomes so the person doesn't have to hold and mentally weigh them, and explicitly elicit values so the choice is checked against them rather than against surface cues.
population: patients facing health treatment/screening decisions (adults, general population), 105 RCTs
context: field RCTs in clinical decision-making settings

implications.text: A decision-table/decision-aid feature should explicitly surface options × attributes × how each maps to Sam's stated priorities/values, not just facts — the values-congruence gain in the literature comes from linking options to values, not just informing.

observation: A large registered-report RCT (N>2,300) comparing 'fact box' tables vs the same medical risk information in prose text found tables produced more comprehension and slightly better knowledge recall at 6 weeks, and were rated more engaging, but showed no difference between formats on actual treatment decisions, feeling informed, or trust.
claim: Tabular presentation reliably beats prose for extracting and retaining discrete facts (comprehension/recall), but format alone does not change which decision people make or how informed/trusting they feel — the decision itself depends on more than presentation format.
mechanism: Tables align comparable attributes on a shared axis, lowering the cost of extracting and comparing individual facts (consistent with information-scent/alignability accounts), but the actual choice is driven by values and stakes that formatting doesn't touch.

implications.text: Use tables for the comprehension/comparison layer of a decision (facts, attributes, numbers) but don't expect the table alone to produce a 'better' decision or more trust — pair it with explicit values-elicitation per F23-03.

observation: UX synthesis (uxtigers.com, drawing on the alignable-differences literature) states that comparison tables work because every row places all alternatives on one shared dimension ('alignable difference'), and alignable differences dominate choice and memory over unalignable ones; well-designed comparison tables are described as functioning as 'decision machines' that should deliver a verdict, not just display data.
claim: The design value of a comparison table comes specifically from forcing attributes into alignable rows/columns; a table that lists each option's own idiosyncratic attributes (unalignable) loses most of the benefit.
mechanism: Alignable differences reduce the cognitive cost of computing a comparison because the same computation (compare value X across options) can be reused row to row; unalignable attributes require constructing a new comparison schema for each item.
population: general (practitioner synthesis, not a primary study)

implications.text: FT-decision-table should normalise/force a shared attribute schema across options (pad missing attributes explicitly as 'unknown' rather than omitting rows) so every comparison stays alignable.

observation: Levin, Schneider & Gaeth (1998) distinguish attribute framing (describing a single attribute of one option as, e.g., '80% lean' vs '20% fat') from goal framing and risky-choice framing; attribute framing reliably shifts evaluation of that attribute (positive frames evaluated more favourably) without changing the underlying facts, and is described as the most robust/simplest of the three framing effect types.
claim: How a single attribute is worded (not just which attributes are shown) measurably changes a decider's evaluation of an option, independent of the actual numbers — a live risk for any auto-generated decision-table copy.
mechanism: Positive/negative wording of the same fact triggers different affective/associative reactions even when the referent value is unchanged.
population: general adult (lab experiments, multiple replications since 1998)

implications.text: When Riemann auto-generates attribute labels/descriptions for a decision table, it must use neutral or dual-valence phrasing (e.g. '80% lean / 20% fat' together) rather than picking one frame, or it silently biases Sam's decision.

observation: The original ego-depletion literature (self-control as a depletable resource, underlying the popular 'decision fatigue' narrative) failed to replicate in a preregistered multilab Registered Replication Report (Hagger et al. 2016, 23 labs, N=2,141), which found a pooled effect of approximately d=0.04, indistinguishable from zero.
claim: The strong causal claim that making many decisions depletes a fixed mental resource that degrades later decision quality ('decision fatigue' as a distinct depletable-willpower mechanism) is not well supported by rigorous replication; treat 'decision fatigue' as at best a redescription of ordinary fatigue/low motivation, not a validated distinct mechanism.
mechanism: unknown / likely publication bias and flexible analysis in the original small-sample studies rather than a real depletable-resource mechanism.

implications.text: Don't design Riemann around a strong 'decision budget' model (e.g. rationing how many decisions Sam can face per day based on a depletion theory); if ordering/timing of decisions matters, treat it as ordinary attention/motivation variation (A17), not a separate depletable-willpower construct.

observation: Marx, Hacker, Yu, Cortese & Sonuga-Barke (2021, J. Attention Disorders) meta-analysed 37 group comparisons (3,763 participants, 53% ADHD) across simple choice-delay and temporal discounting paradigms and found small-to-medium effect sizes: people with ADHD choose small-immediate over larger-delayed rewards more often than controls, with the effect roughly doubling in odds ratio when real (vs hypothetical) rewards were used.
claim: ADHD is robustly associated with steeper delay discounting / stronger preference for immediate over delayed rewards, and this bias is stronger when stakes are concrete/real rather than hypothetical — relevant to any decision involving a delayed payoff (e.g. 'decide now vs gather more info first').
mechanism: Steeper delay-of-reinforcement gradient in ADHD reduces the subjective value assigned to delayed outcomes relative to neurotypical controls, especially under real (motivationally salient) incentives.
population: children/adolescents and adults with ADHD, meta-analysis
context: meta-analysis of lab choice-delay and discounting tasks

implications.text: When a decision table involves a delayed-benefit option (e.g. 'wait for a better offer', 'save vs spend now'), Riemann should make the delayed payoff concrete and salient (numbers, dates) rather than abstract, since abstract/hypothetical framing under-weights delayed value even more for an ADHD user.

observation: Assumption A29 (detail from the original is valuable in itself) was '?' for the decide objective. Research on information overload in consumer decisions (Stevens Institute of Technology lab studies) and the fact-box RCT (F23-04) both indicate that additional facts beyond what's needed to compare options degrade decision quality/satisfaction rather than improving it, while the Cochrane decision-aid review (F23-03) shows benefit comes from structured, values-linked information, not raw original-text detail.
claim: Resolves A29×decide: original/raw detail is NOT independently valuable for deciding; what matters is decision-relevant, comparable detail (the attributes that differentiate the live options), and detail beyond that measurably hurts satisfaction and adds noise. A29×decide should resolve to N, not C or Y.
mechanism: Decisions are optimised by minimising the cost of comparing the attributes that actually differentiate live alternatives; irrelevant original-text detail adds search/comparison cost without adding discriminating power.
context: mixed lab experiments + RCT + systematic review

implications.text: FT-decision-table should default to showing only attributes that differ across the live options (a diff-oriented table), with an explicit expand-to-original-detail affordance for the rare case Sam wants it, rather than defaulting to full original text.

observation: Assumption A20 (proactive surfacing wanted) was '?' for decide. Field research on proactive AI reminder/nudge systems (e.g. Viva Daily Briefing commitment-detection study; a 5-day field study of developer interaction with proactive AI; a preference-aligned proactive-assistant study) consistently finds that the value of unprompted surfacing is highest for small, low-stakes, easily-forgotten items, and that user reaction turns negative specifically when the system intervenes at a bad time, without enough user control, or in an unwanted style/channel — independent of whether the content itself was useful.
claim: Resolves A20×decide: proactive surfacing of a due decision is conditionally wanted (C), not simply Y or N — it should hold only when Riemann can time it well and give Sam control over the interruption (matching existing A16/A17 timing and A19 one-tap-input pattern), and works best for low-stakes/easily-missed decisions rather than high-stakes ones where the interruption cost itself is a distinct source of dissatisfaction.
mechanism: Proactive value comes from filling a gap the user would otherwise have to remember to check themselves (external cognitive offload), but the cost is an attention interruption; net benefit flips negative when timing/control/style are wrong, regardless of content relevance.
context: field studies of proactive AI assistants (workplace)

implications.text: A due-decision surfacing feature should be gated by the same interrupt-tier logic already planned for monitor (FT-interrupt-tiers) rather than treated as a separate always-on nudge, and should default to low-friction/dismissible presentation.

observation: Information foraging theory (Pirolli & Card, summarised by Pirolli 1999/2007 and NN/g's applied synthesis) models information-seeking as maximising the rate of gain (information value / cost), guided by 'information scent' — the perceived cues (titles, keywords, surrounding text) that predict whether following a link/patch will pay off; users abandon low-scent paths quickly (satisficing) rather than exhaustively searching.
claim: For known-item lookup, the representation that minimises time-to-fact is one that maximises information scent at each navigation step (precise, query-matching labels/headers) and lets the user jump directly to the located passage — not a compressed summary, which by construction discards the scent cues (exact terms, structure) a scent-based searcher relies on.
mechanism: Foraging efficiency depends on scent cues correlating with true relevance at low cost; summarisation strips the specific wording/structure that carries scent, forcing the user back to the source anyway once a candidate is found.
population: general web/information users; foraging theory has broad HCI support but few controlled A/B comparisons of 'summary vs search+highlight' specifically

implications.text: FT-reference-lookup should be built as search-plus-jump-to-highlighted-source (preserve original wording/structure and let full-text search find it), not as a pre-generated summary layer — a summary is actively worse for known-item lookup because it destroys scent cues and still requires a return to source.

observation: The exploratory-search literature (Marchionini; White & Roth; Athukorala et al. 2016 JASIST comparison of search behaviour on exploratory vs lookup tasks) distinguishes known-item/lookup tasks — a single fact or document satisfies the goal, analytic query-based strategies dominate — from exploratory search, where the goal itself is unclear and browsing/iterative strategies dominate; interfaces optimised for one style measurably hurt the other.
claim: A summary is well-matched to exploratory/orientation goals (where the user doesn't know exactly what they need) but is the wrong tool for known-item retrieval (where the user already knows the target and just needs to reach it fast) — these are different tasks needing different Riemann affordances, not one lookup UI serving both.
mechanism: Lookup tasks are satisfied by precision and directness to a single answer; exploratory tasks are satisfied by breadth, comparison and serendipitous discovery — optimising an interface for recall/breadth (a summary tree) adds friction to a lookup task that needs a direct hit.
population: general information searchers, lab and behavioural log studies
context: lab studies + literature review, information retrieval/HCI

implications.text: Riemann needs to distinguish a 'reference/lookup' mode (search bar into full text, jump-to-hit) from the zoom-dial abstraction tree (built for orientation/understanding); routing a known-item query through the abstraction tree instead of search is a mismatch.

observation: Whittaker & Sidner (1996, 'Email Overload: Exploring Personal Information Management of Email') found email inboxes are 'overloaded' in function: used simultaneously for communication, task management (to-dos), and personal archiving, which is why volume alone doesn't capture the problem — the mixed status types (to-do, to-read, to-archive) sitting undifferentiated in one list is the core issue.
claim: Email overload is a triage/classification problem (undifferentiated status types in one stream) as much as a volume problem; a briefing tool that only compresses text without separating action-required from FYI from archival content doesn't address the actual overload mechanism identified in the foundational study.
mechanism: Cognitive cost comes from repeatedly re-scanning a mixed-status list to figure out what state each item is in, not from reading volume per se.
population: knowledge workers, field study of email use
context: field study, foundational CSCW/CHI work, revisited 10 years later with similar conclusions

implications.text: FT-reply-brief should first classify what an email/thread IS (action-required with an ask, FYI, archival) before compressing it, mirroring Whittaker & Sidner's status-type distinction, rather than treating all threads as one kind of summarisation target.

observation: Dabbish & Kraut (2006, CSCW, 'Email Overload at Work') found perceived email overload is driven by email volume moderated by management strategy, and follow-up work (Kushlev & Dunn 2015) found that checking email less frequently reduced stress but did NOT reduce, and sometimes increased, perceived overload, because deferred/unhandled items accumulate and must still be triaged later.
claim: Reducing check-frequency (batching) lowers moment-to-moment stress but does not by itself solve overload; any batching feature must also reduce the triage cost of the accumulated backlog when it's finally opened, or it just relocates the overload rather than reducing it.
mechanism: Overload is a function of backlog size and triage cost per item; deferring consumption without reducing per-item triage cost only delays and concentrates the cost.
population: working adults, field surveys and diary/experience-sampling studies
context: field study + field experiment, workplace email use

implications.text: If Riemann batches communication (aligning with FT-batching from earlier reports), the batched view still needs FT-reply-brief-style per-item triage compression (ask, deadline, context at a glance) — batching alone is not sufficient.

observation: Hancock, Naaman & Levy (2020, J. Computer-Mediated Communication) define AI-Mediated Communication (AI-MC) as an intelligent agent operating on behalf of a communicator by modifying, augmenting, or generating messages, and argue this requires re-evaluating existing CMC trust/authenticity theories rather than assuming AI-assisted messages behave like human-authored ones.
claim: Any Riemann feature that drafts or shapes what Sam sends to someone else (even just briefing what to say) is operating in a space where the literature explicitly flags novel trust/perception risks — this is not a neutral compression task the way summarising for oneself is.
mechanism: unknown — the paper is a framework/research agenda, not an effect-size study.
population: general (theoretical framework paper, cites empirical AI-MC studies)

implications.text: FT-reply-brief must stay a briefing aide (surface the ask/deadline/context for Sam to write from) rather than drafting finished sender-voice text, consistent with the 'Sam sends' scope constraint (A28) and this paper's warning that AI-shaped messages carry distinct trust dynamics.

observation: Jakesch et al. (2019, CHI, AI-MC trust study) found people distrusted AI-suspected-written profiles only in a mixed-set condition where some profiles were AI-written and some human-written and evaluators could contrast them ('Replicant Effect') — not when they saw AI-written profiles in isolation. A 2025 follow-up (Purcell, Jakesch et al., N=1,637 in trust games) found AI predictive-text assistance had minimal impact on trust regardless of disclosure, and let people compose equally trust-inducing messages faster.
claim: AI assistance in composing a message to someone else does not inherently damage trust and can save time without a trust penalty, but a penalty can appear specifically when the recipient can compare AI-assisted vs unassisted messages side by side — a comparison-triggered effect, not a blanket AI-authorship penalty.
mechanism: Distrust of AI-written text arises from social inference under contrast (readers infer something about why one profile 'needed' AI help when they can compare), not from the presence of AI assistance per se.
population: general adult (Airbnb-profile and trust-game lab/online experiments)

implications.text: A briefing/reply-support feature is on safer ground than a full auto-draft feature: it keeps Sam as the visible author (no contrast condition where a recipient could detect 'this one was AI, this one wasn't'), avoiding the Replicant Effect risk entirely.

observation: EmailSum (Zhang et al. 2021, ACL, 2,549 annotated email threads with short (<30 words) and long (<100 words) reference summaries) found that even fine-tuned models scoring well on automatic metrics regularly fail at two specific things: understanding sender intent ('what the thread is mainly about' / why it was sent) and correctly attributing 'who does what to whom' across participants — automatic metrics (ROUGE) correlate poorly with human judgment of these failures.
claim: Extracting 'the ask' from an email thread is a known hard case for automatic summarisation, specifically failing on intent and speaker/role attribution, not just length compression — a reply-brief feature needs targeted ask/role extraction, not generic summarisation, and needs human-graded (not ROUGE-based) evaluation.
mechanism: Generic summarisation optimises for salient-content coverage, not for the specific pragmatic structure (who is asking whom for what, by when) that a reply-brief needs.

implications.text: FT-reply-brief needs a dedicated ask/deadline/role extraction pass (structured fields: who is asking, what for, by when, what context) plus a faithfulness check specific to those fields, not a generic length-based summary — reuse the faithfulness-check pattern from FT-faithfulness-score but target these fields.

observation: The curse-of-knowledge / audience-design literature (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber 1989; applied to visual data communication by Xiong et al.) shows people who know something well systematically overestimate how salient/obvious that information will be to someone who doesn't share their knowledge, including in choosing what to include/omit when summarising for others.
claim: When Riemann helps Sam brief someone else (or vice versa, brief Sam on someone else's message), the compression step has a specific, well-documented failure mode: silently dropping context the sender/expert finds obvious but the reader needs — this is a distinct risk from ordinary information loss and needs an explicit check.
mechanism: Experts' mental models compress background/context automatically and unconsciously, so they don't register it as needing to be stated when producing a summary for someone else.
population: general adult, mixed lab studies (expert/novice communication, data visualization)

implications.text: FT-reply-brief should include a recipient-context field ('what does the other person already know / not know') that Riemann prompts for or infers, rather than assuming the thread content alone determines what to include.

observation: Sarrafzadeh et al. (2019, CHIIR, 'Exploring Email Triage') and the companion 'Characterizing and Predicting Email Deferral Behavior' study found users are more likely to defer emails specifically when handling requires replying, careful reading, or clicking attachments/links, and that deferral is driven by perceived response effort and current workload rather than sender importance alone (though sender importance is also a factor).
claim: The specific class of email that gets deferred (and therefore piles up as overload) is reply-requiring, effort-heavy email — exactly the class a reply-brief feature should target first, since it's both the highest-value and the most avoided category.
mechanism: Deferral is a cost-avoidance response to perceived effort; lowering the perceived/actual effort of composing a reply (via a brief that states the ask, deadline, context) should reduce deferral for this category specifically.
population: knowledge workers, large-scale log study (enterprise email)

implications.text: Prioritise FT-reply-brief for threads that require a reply (not FYI/read-only threads) — this is the highest-leverage subset per the deferral-behavior data, and briefing reduces exactly the 'perceived effort' variable shown to drive deferral.
